relevance_note: This is a literature review of patients with HA20, which it defines as "caused by a heterozygous mutation in the TNFAIP3 gene"; it is mostly aggregate (Table 1: 74 East Asian and 51 other patients) but describes four individuals with clinical detail (e.g. "The first case of allogeneic HCT was a 14-year-old English boy."), none with an individually attributed variant.
method_note: Read the whole paper manually; the JSON was assembled with a short Python script from values I chose, and the script checked every span verbatim against the paper and every row against the schema fields. The paper is a review: Table 1 holds only aggregate counts (columns 'East Asia' and 'without East Asia'), so no per-patient table was transcribed. Individuals: only people singled out with clinical detail were recorded: the two allogeneic-HCT cases (14-year-old English boy, 6-year-old Japanese boy), the patient who received autologous HCT for CNS vasculitis (ref 30), and the East Asian patient who developed Hodgkin lymphoma (ref 10). All four come from previously published reports. The two allogeneic-HCT cases are cited jointly as '(31, 47)', so source_reference_in_review is '(31, 47)' for both; the paper does not assign one reference to each. The paper's own statements suggest English boy = ref 31 (other regions) and Japanese boy = ref 47 (East Asia; ref 47 is also cited for the only East Asian patient given canakinumab), but this is not stated outright. Not recorded as separate people, to avoid inventing or duplicating people: 'only one patient in East Asia showed elevated ISG expression (47)' (possibly the same as the Japanese boy, not stated) and 'Only one patient was treated with anti-IL-1 agents (canakinumab) in East Asia (47)' / 'Anti-IL-1 agents were administered to one patient with HA20 in East Asia and were not effective' (by the paper's own logic this is the Japanese boy, who was refractory to canakinumab; not used). The label 'One patient with HA20 in East Asia' means only the Hodgkin lymphoma patient (ref 10). It was not merged with anyone. Variants: the paper names variants only at study or family level (Cys243Tyr (45), Glu192Lys (18), Met476Ile (20), Arg183X in two families (22, 27), Arg87X (21, 42), p.Asn102Ser, c.487-1G>A, p.Val309dup, and the polymorphism Phe127Cys/rs2230926). None is attributed to an individual, so the variants table is empty. Ages '14-year-old' and '6-year-old' are the only ages given and were recorded as age at last evaluation/time of report; they may be ages at HCT. n_patients_reported = 125 is the sum of the two stated counts (74 East Asia + 51 other regions; the paper gives no single total). Checklist choices kept to explicit statements: 'enteropathy' and 'bowel disease' were not mapped to 'gastrointestinal ulcers or inflammation', 'hepatitis' not to 'autoimmune hepatitis', 'cell depletion' not to 'cytopenia (autoimmune)', and 'Hodgkin lymphoma' not to 'lymphoproliferation or lymphadenopathy'; all are left 'not reported'. 'insulin-dependent DM' -> type 1 diabetes, 'frequent fever' -> recurrent fever, 'psoriasis' -> skin lesions, 'central nervous system vasculitis' -> CNS involvement and vasculitis. No features are explicitly excluded for any individual. Internal inconsistency in the paper: it says four potential splice-site/duplication mutations were unevaluated, then 'One of these mutations was reported in Japan (16), while four were reported in China (25, 27)' (1 + 4 = 5). Also Table 1 gives 42/51 as 82.6% (arithmetically 82.4%). Neither affects the extracted rows.

study_type.span: In this review, we summarize the characteristics of patients with HA20 in East Asia and compare these with patients in other regions

span: A total of 74 patients in 39 families were affected by HA20 in East Asia
a total of 51 patients in 23 families were affected by HA20 in other regions
We summarized the literature on patients with HA20 resulting from TNFAIP3 mutations starting from the first report of this disease in 2016 until August 2021.
A total of 20 studies in East Asia and 15 studies in other regions, mainly the USA and Europe, were published during this period (10–44).
